But this gentleman had given the proper shade of meaning to every thought I had tried to put into the minds of those people at that time.
I imagine that when setting up a plan of immediate interpretation in this country there might be a little difficulty in finding interpreters of that type. Perhaps you could find interpreters who could immediately convert spoken English into French, and French into English. But they would not have had the same practice as they have in Europe where there are so many small countries talking different languages. So there may be some difficulty. But it is not impossible. I do not think this has anything to do with bilingualism. That matter was all settled at the time of confederation. There are bilingual rights in this house, and since those rights exist I think the best possible facilities should be taken advantage of at the earliest opportunity.
House of Commons
I am certainly in favour of the resolution, and if I have the privilege of being here when the matter is finally discussed and considered, I will support it. I take it, from what the minister has said, that it will not be possible to deal with the matter this session, and that even if a committee were set up now it would need to have the authority to continue on into another session and discuss the matter further. I quite agree that it is logical to contend it cannot be finished this session, but I think it is all to the good that as many of us who can do so should express our views on this subject, and if these views are as unanimous, as they have been up to the moment, then I think we can find ways of making it possible for all of us to understand at all times what is being said in this house by providing the facilities for simultaneous translation of speeches which can be heard at the same time in English and French.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO STUDY SYSTEM OF SIMULTANEOUS TRANSLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank the leader of the house for having given hon. members on this side an opportunity for discussing this subject notwithstanding that he had already moved the adjournment. There are still a number of speakers who would like to discuss this resolution, and I was among those myself. That is one of the reasons, along with others, why I intervened at the time I did. I want, together with those who have risen on this side of the house, to support at this time the motion made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Breton) and I do this not only because of the fact that I believe a simultaneous translation of the debates in this house would be a good thing, but also because I believe that the resolution does answer at least some of the objections which were raised earlier during the course of the debate.
The resolution, in my opinion, is a very simple one. It states that the house-
. . . should take into consideration the advisability of setting up a special committee of parliament for the purpose of considering the establishment of a system of simultaneous translation, in the official language which is not that used by the member then speaking, for all debates in the House of Commons and in all parliamentary committees.
A question was asked of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) not long ago to which his reply was: "Yes, we are willing to consider anything," and I am sure that this would apply to the resolution which is now before the house.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) after making a contribution to the debate I think said in effect that the idea of studying the question is a good one. That was also said by the Secretary of State (Mrs. Fair-clough) who, while perhaps she did not use

House of Commons
the same language, said that the Speaker has the matter under consideration. I think, too, that the leader of the house in rising earlier to make the contribution he did used words to the effect that the government was anxious to give this sympathetic consideration but that perhaps this was not the method by which to do it.
The point I would like to make at this time is this. With but few exceptions most of those who have risen to take part in this debate seem to me to have favoured the resolution. Well, that being the case it would strike me there should be no objection to accepting the resolution in its present state because of the statements that have been made by those who have taken part in the debate.
I realize that the point made by the house leader at the present time is perhaps one which could be useful on other occasions but I do not know that it is as useful on this occasion because, after all, this is private members' day. This day is devoted to private members' resolutions and whether we speak until ten o'clock on this or whether we do not I think makes no difference to the government. Of course, I am not suggesting by that statement that we are going to do that. I would rather approve of what the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) said, that after the contributions which we intend to make are made the motion made by the leader of the house will be taken up by the house. But it would strike me that because of the arguments that have been made by most of those who have risen to speak in the debate the resolution should be accepted by the government.
There have been some objections raised but in my opinion they were not very serious and all of them could be studied by the committee that this resolution seeks to establish. I think of the objection raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). He could go to this committee personally and give the benefit of his advice as an electrician or in any other capacity he may wish so the committee would have in its possession all the information capable of enabling it to arrive at a decision on the important question that is now before us.
As other hon. members who have spoken today stated, I too have had the advantage and the privilege of sitting at the United Nations. In fact, I had the great honour of leading the Canadian delegation in 1948 when that delegation sat at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris. During those six or seven weeks while I was there I was astounded at the rapidity, the fluency and the accuracy with which the simultaneous translation went on. It seems to me that those who are anxious to

learn and speak the French language would have a greater advantage in so doing if the simultaneous translation system were to be adopted in this chamber.
In my experience in coming back to the house after an absence of three years I was astounded when listening to some hon. members from the province of Quebec particularly at the manner in which they had improved their English. I hesitate to mention any names but I was more than surprised to observe that in this short period of time several hon. members were able to speak almost perfect English and I think I can pay the same compliment to some hon. members on the other side of the house whose ability to speak French has improved. I was astounded and pleased as well to see how some hon. members not from the province of Quebec on the other side of the house could rise and speak good French. I will not say it is excellent French but it is good French. Simultaneous translation will not only assist but will tremendously improve that facility because, as has been said here by the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson), if a person is speaking in one language, let us say the English language, and one wants to listen to the speech in French he can turn on the translation and follow the speech from one language to the other.
As the Secretary of State said, it may be that it would be difficult to obtain translators but I doubt that very much because I know there are Canadians at the United Nations now who are serving as translators and they have had little or no difficulty in performing that service. I have no doubt that translators could be obtained from the Department of the Secretary of State or from other sources outside of the department altogether.
I say to my hon. friend the leader of the house that if most of those who have risen and spoken on this resolution favour it, what objection could there be to the government accepting it, considering it and studying it? I agree with him there is not much time left from now to the end of the session but I do not think anyone either on this side or on the other side of the house would think for one moment that all the information required on the part of the government to make a decision on this resolution could be obtained within the next four or five weeks.
It is the establishment of the committee which is important. The Speaker I presume would want to be represented on it. Indeed I do not think a committee of this nature could be established and report properly without some representation from the Speaker

and from the office of the Secretary of State. That is why I submit with deference to my hon. friend that perhaps instead of moving the motion he did he might well give consideration to the establishment of the committee. I think he would please most hon. members in so doing and certainly he would please the majority who have taken part in this debate. For these reasons I invite him to give consideration to the establishment of the committee as set out in the motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say only a few words. I do not wish unduly to protract this discussion since the opportunity to support the request of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm in favour of the establishment of a committee must be given not only to the government but to all the members of this house.
Some members opposite who have taken part in this debate have held that Mr. Speaker should be asked to make a personal study of this matter. I believe that the motion of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm is very clear. It requests the establishment of a special parliamentary committee to study the means of establishment of a system of simultaneous translation. It is obvious that such a parliamentary committee must be made up of members who sit in this house, Mr. Speaker included, if he so wishes.
I can see no possible objection to the establishment of that committee. On the contrary, this proposal is a further argument in favour of the establishment of a simultaneous interpretation system.
I believe that the point made by the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) is the soundest yet. He pointed out that with simultaneous translation a speaker who wishes to take part in a debate can immediately take up a subject discussed by the previous speaker and continue the same discussion in his own mother tongue. I believe that is one of the soundest points made and one which we should stress when we ask the government to set up this committee so that the house may enjoy that improvement at as early a date as possible.
In my opinion it is a mistake to claim that simultaneous interpretation would prevent certain English-speaking or French-speaking members to practise speaking in a language other than their own. In fact conversation is the logical adjunct of French lessons, and this would be one way for those members who are studying French to find out immediately how they are coming along. To me, that seems a worthwhile argument.
House of Commons
When I was a boy and when I was learning to use a shotgun or rifle, I was told: "Watch out, the gun kicks". Well that gun has been kicking a great deal this afternoon, as I was listening to the speeches made by the members for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard), who expressed the opinion that in previous sessions the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm had not displayed the same zeal in this matter.
The motion proposed by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm was put on the order paper during the last session. However, it never came up for debate because there were too many motions ahead of it, and those proposed resolutions must be studied one at a time and not all together. That is what is happening today. It so happens that his notice of motion is on top of the list. When there are 55 on the order paper, it would be unreasonable to require that they all be discussed at the same session. In fact, that is what happened to somebody who showed a great deal of zeal as regards family allowances during one particular election. I remember that a motion dreamed up by the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) during an election in the constituency of Temiscouata, with regard to the increase in family allowances, never came up for discussion in the house simply because its turn never came.
I believe that my hon. friends from Lotbiniere and St. Hyacinthe should have remembered this kickback, before expressing doubts about the zeal of the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm with regard to the discussion of his resolution.

I am pleased to give my full support to the resolution moved by my hon. friend.
This afternoon, speakers stressed the usefulness of the system for members themselves, but I should like for a few minutes to insist on the advantages that the system would also have for listeners in the galleries.
When I attended the meetings of the General Assembly of the United Nations last year in New York I knew that a system of simultaneous translation was provided for the delegates but I did not know then that visitors in the galleries and the numerous visitors in the United Nations building in New York, could also follow, in their own language, the debates that were going on either in the General Assembly or in the various committees.
I also know that the Canadian government contributed financially to the installation of the system used in the United Nations building and I wonder why the many visitors that we sometimes have in this house could not also follow the debates in their own language. I remember once taking about fifty students to the galleries where they spent part of the afternoon listening to the debates. When I saw them again later that afternoon, I found that they were a bit disappointed because, as they were all French-speaking, hardly any of them had understood a single word of the speeches made. I conclude that it would be advantageous for the members as well as for the voters of Canada who come to the House of Commons in fairly great numbers if they had the privilege of following the debates in their own language.
It can be said that some organizations in this country have already benefited from this simultaneous translation in their national conventions. We know that, at their national congress, the chambers of commerce had made the discussions easier for their delegates by

means of such a system. I believe that one labour organization also insisted on providing its delegates at a national convention with a system of simultaneous translation. We might be surprised to know the number of national organizations which apply to the International Civil Aviation Organization in Montreal for the use of its hall, which is already equipped with such a system.
Well, Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, we heard only one member who was opposed to the establishment of such a system, because, according to him, it would be too costly; [ refer to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who is, I believe, the only member of his party who has expressed his opinion in the house today, and who declared himself against the resolution of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I do not wish to extend this debate. I am pleased to offer my hearty congratulations to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and tell him that it is with very great pleasure that I shall vote in favour of his motion.

I was saying, that the Prime Minister made a point of speaking French at every opportunity and that he respects the French language, which is a fine example to be given to young Canadians; and his example has been followed by several English-speaking members of my party, and during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and ever since, they have addressed this house in French and have managed to do so most creditably. I hope this is only a beginning, and that more and more of our English-speaking colleagues will address the house in French.
Bilingualism is gaining ground every day in Canada, progressing quietly but surely, which constitutes the best way to achieve our national unity.
If we want to live in a prosperous country, a progressive country, it is essential that we should understand one another. There is no better way to be understood by one's own fellow-citizens than to learn the language of other races in our country. Many errors could be avoided if people were always able to understand one another.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that both languages, English and French, are official in the parliament of Canada. This was the wish of the fathers of confederation, a wish always fully respected by all political parties and all governments which have succeeded each other since confederation. Unfortunately, it is inevitable that most of our Frenchspeaking members are somewhat reluctant to

address this house in their mother tongue for they know full well that a great many of their colleagues cannot understand what is being said and have to wait until the next day to read the translation of the debates. That is also why English-speaking members who cannot speak French regret their inability to understand and follow with interest the statements and contributions of their French-speaking colleagues, and this is very often a source of confusion which can give rise to misunderstanding and very unpleasant consequences.
As a matter of fact, it is not the first time that the question of simultaneous translation has been brought up in this house. Every year, motions, resolutions or contributions are introduced either during the debate on the speech from the throne or the budget debate. But, unfortunately, for the past 20 years, the efforts of the members, under the former government, have always been unavailing. The matter was brought up very often, but the government never saw fit, useful or necessary to take measures to instal such a system.
I am glad tonight to see that the members of the former government, which had not seen fit to bring these improvements to the House of Commons, rise one after the other to stress the necessity of that measure and how glad they would be to see it adopted.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO STUDY SYSTEM OF SIMULTANEOUS TRANSLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was expressing my admiration just as was done by the ministers of the former government who have now come to the conclusion that such a measure could be useful and could promote national unity.

However, such a system has already been tried for some years by all the great international organizations of which Canada is a member. Thus, at the United Nations, there is a system of simultaneous translation in the five official languages of that organization. I really believe that if it was found possible to establish such a system at the United Nations, for simultaneous interpretation in five different official languages, it would be equally possible to establish the same system for the two official languages in this house. This system which was installed in the United Nations is, as a matter of fact, the same as will be found at NATO and at different international gatherings.
In Canada it is at present used for various meetings of chambers of commerce, industrial groups and others. It is generally agreed that it does away with a great many errors and allows Canadians to know each other better by making it easier for them to express their own ideas in their own native tongue.
As you know, there was a meeting last summer of the International Postal Union, here in Ottawa. A system of simultaneous translation had been installed in the House of Commons for that meeting. Once this conference was over, the government considered the possibility of keeping that system permanently. Unfortunately, that system had been made specially for that conference. Moreover, it had been installed hastily, it was much too cumbersome and it would really have altered the appearance of the House of Commons. It was then that the matter was referred to the internal economy committee of the house, where it is under consideration. We are following on this matter the very procedure that was followed when the microphone system which we now have was installed. I well remember that for years members in various parts of the house had been complaining about the acoustics. Unfortunately, several members were afraid that the installations of a microphone system would mar the appearance of the house and that is why the solution of the problem took so much time.
The house is provided with an amplifier system which, although detracting to some extent from the beauty of this chamber, allows us to hear clearly the speeches being delivered, and although this system is rather costly, generally speaking, the business of the house is being carried on much more 96698-954
House of Commons
efficiently. For this reason, the study of a simultaneous translation system for the house has been entrusted to the internal economy committee, which had already considered the establishment of our amplifier system.
It is purely and simply a technical question. We are all in agreement on that. All political parties in the house recognize the official use of both languages here. All members recognize that each and everyone of them has the right to address the house in either one of our two official languages.
The matter now before the internal economy committee is not one that concerns bilingualism but rather the technical aspect of the problem. It is a matter of determining what system of simultaneous translation would be the best for the house and what the cost would be of such a system. We must also find out whether it would be possible to use the present public address system. The thing is to know if we are going to have a system including devices as heavy as those that were installed at the United Nations five or six years ago or smaller sets which can be fitted over the ears and are nearly invisible. We must also determine what type of installation we are going to have for oral translation, how many interpreters would be required and what salary they should get. All these matters have now been referred to the internal economy committee. So far the committee has gathered a good deal of information and it shall continue to study the matter. I hope it will be in a position to submit a report to the house at the earliest opportunity.
The resolution now before the house asks that this matter be referred to a committee of the house. Well, Mr. Speaker, this session will be of short duration and there would be no point in setting up committees, since within three or four weeks the session will be over. All those who are anxious that such a new step be taken should have confidence in the internal economy committee. Besides, that was the body which gave us the amplifier system we now use and it will be the one, I am convinced, to give the house a system of simultaneous translation.
The motion now before the house calls precisely for what the internal economy committee is now achieving. I do not see how the setting up of a committee of the house of Commons would in any way hasten this project, for we know from past experience

House of Commons
that a committee of the house, where all parties are represented, always takes some time before it gets going and that it follows a rather complicated procedure, during which each member wants to express his own views, which generally leads to a lengthy debate. This is a purely technical, and not a political matter.
Everybody is agreed on the constitutional question of bilingualism in this house. This is simply a matter for experts. The aim is to get technical information such as only engineers can give. I do not know that fifteen or twenty members of parliament seated around a table, who are all in favour of simultaneous translation and listening to information by experts in acoustics or in simultaneous translation, can possibly hasten the introduction of some system of simultaneous translation, which everybody in this country looks upon with such favour and which could render such excellent service. The setting up of such a committee would probably delay the study of this matter.
I sincerely believe that we are going in the right direction and that the internal economy committee will be in a position to submit a technical report to the house, and I am convinced that before long we shall have in the house a simultaneous translation system, so that the principle of integral bilingualism in the Canadian parliament may cease to be a mere theory in the constitution to become a practical reality.
I sincerely believe that this would help Canadian unity, as well as the debates, for it is highly advantageous that everyone should be understood at once without having to wait until Hansard is translated; it often happens as we know, that due to certain circumstances, the French copy of Hansard is published with a few hours' delay. I am convinced that it is possible to find technical means which will allow simultaneous interpretation to be given in this house without changing	in the least its traditional
appearance.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of such a system and I would like to ask all those who have spoken so far to have confidence in the house's internal economy committee. I am convinced that before long there will be simultaneous interpretation in this house when the board's report is brought down.

Mr. Speaker, as has already been indicated by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) some of us do have certain doubts about the wisdom or desirability of a simultaneous translation system for this House of Commons. The reason for these doubts has already been expressed- some of us fear the innovation might have the effect of making debates in this house too mechanical. We fear, also, that it might discourage some of us whose mother tongue is English from trying to learn the other official language of this country.
House of Commons
We are also somewhat amazed, as are hon. members opposite, at the great interest now being shown in this question by supporters of the Liberal party, in view of the silence they held on this issue in years gone by. However, Mr. Speaker, what is before us, while it is to a large extent a discussion of a simultaneous translation system, is only a motion that the government give consideration to the setting up of a committee to give further consideration to the matter, and it seems to me that whether one is for or against the installation of a simultaneous translation system it is only fair to have the matter looked into by a committee which could make a much better study and examination of the matter than can be achieved through the kind of discussion we are having today.
I was a little surprised at the stand taken by the government as expressed by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) and also by the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) on this matter, namely that it should not be referred to a committee, but rather that we should trust the various departments of government which are looking into the question to go into it satisfactorily. I suppose we will have occasion many times to come back to a phrase which was used a good deal during the election campaign-"the supremacy of parliament".
As far as the arrangements of the House of Commons are concerned, surely that is something for the House of Commons as a whole, rather than for the government to decide. I realize that if the expenditure of money is involved then the government has to come into the picture, but at the initial stage, namely the studying of the question to decide whether or not hon. members as a whole will want to look further into this proposal, I suggest that parliament should be supreme, and that this investigation should be undertaken by a committee of the House of Commons rather than leave it to a department or departments of government.
You will notice that I do not speak in the same terms with respect to the fact that Your Honour is making a study of the question. You, sir, are the servant of the house and I put your study in a different category from the study being made by any department of the government. It seems to me that the very fact that Your Honour is making a study of the matter puts it down as a parliamentary question and infers that there should therefore be a committee of parliament, with Your Honour as a member, to examine into this issue.
I speak as one who is not yet convinced that a simultaneous translation system would be a good idea. I am concerned about the

House of Commons
mechanical results that might be produced. I think, too, that some of us might lose the incentive to acquire greater facility in the other official language.
But in the meantime, because of the interest shown in the question on all sides of the house, I think that no matter what our views may be on the ultimate question we should be able to get together with regard to the desirability of having a committee look into the matter. As I indicated by the question I put to the Minister of Public Works when he was speaking, I do not feel that it is any serious objection to the motion to say that there is no time for a committee to be set up at the present session. The motion does not ask for that. The motion asks for consideration to be given to the setting up of a committee. So, Mr. Speaker, I hope we will not be carried away from the terms of the motion, but, rather, that we will remind ourselves that all it proposes is that a committee be directed to look further into this matter. Surely that is a reasonable request.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a brief word to say. I have had some experience with resolutions. In 1937 I had a resolution before the house and there was a full dress debate on health insurance. I had a resolution on last session dealing with increased pensions for retired civil servants. I have one on again this session, and I expect it will be successful.
The object of bringing in resolutions is to place before the government something which is a national wrong and which ought to be corrected. Mr. Speaker, I strongly support the request for the establishment of a simultaneous translation system. I hope we shall have it soon; it will allow not only the members, but the parliamentary correspondents, the people coming to visit us and our friends who do not speak English, to follow the debates with much more interest.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO STUDY SYSTEM OF SIMULTANEOUS TRANSLATION
speechtext:
In rising to speak on the resolution before the house this evening I approach it from the point of view as a neutral since, having as I do have a command of both languages I do not suffer as undoubtedly a number of members of this house suffer when listening to speeches in a language which is not their own. I can fully understand that those who come from the province of Quebec and who hear speeches in the varying tones and accents of English-and in making this statement I do not cast any reflection on other hon. members for I admit I am to some extent in this category myself-such Quebec members may find a little difficulty in understanding some of the accents with which English is spoken in this house. As I say, I do not reproach hon. members in this respect, but there it is. I can fully appreciate that those members whose mother tongue is French but who have, shall we say, a working knowledge of the English language, might have considerable difficulty in following the full sense of some speeches.
Now if, on the other hand, we look at the other side of the question when hon. members are listening to speeches made by one of the hon. members from the province of Quebec, particularly when they get wound up-and here one must pay tribute to the heights of eloquence which some hon. members from that province can reach-English

speaking members, in turn, do get completely lost. Therefore the tendency is for those members to slip behind the curtain into the lobbies because it must be admitted that it sometimes gets pretty boring listening to something you do not understand.
I feel we all agree with the principle that simultaneous translation offers many advantages, and I must concur in the statement made by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) that perhaps we might have less disagreement with the press as to what actually was said in this house, if all hon. members could actually get the true sense of words spoken at the time they are actually spoken.
I was a little amused this afternoon at the statement made by the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) when he said that when he was speaking in the language not his own he felt the translation was an improvement on his own words. I, too, feel I would be in the same position when speaking in French although I understand that language quite well.
I did point out the other day and I do emphasize again that only approximately 12 per cent of the people of this country are bilingual. Some 67 per cent are reputedly unilingual in that they speak only English and some 20 per cent speak only French.
I certainly deprecate that state of affairs. In this house we recognize in all sincerity, as is recognized in other parts of the country, that there are two official languages in Canada and the great foundation of this nation is laid in the existence of two peoples who have different cultures on which a common culture may be based. We also realize that we will have much greater understanding and will insure the achievement of national unity only if we understand one another.
I would submit that it is only on the basis of knowing of what the other man is speaking and reading what he is writing that we will be able to achieve this end. I sincerely feel that every effort should be made by us to inculcate in our children the love of each other's language. I am not saying we should all learn French only but I feel it would be well if those who are French would also try to learn English so that we may get along with one another. This will serve us not only within our country but beyond its confines. Those members of this house who travel extensively in Europe-whether for reasons of pleasure, private or government business -realize the immense value of the knowledge of at least one other language. We in Canada have the opportunity to speak English
House of Commons
or French or both, and I would commend to the members of this house the understanding and speaking of both languages.
At the moment I would think perhaps that the provision of some mechanical or automatic translation into one's own language of the speeches of members in another language would discourage the learning of that other language. I think there are a number of members of this house who have made some effort to learn French because there is no translation system. We have there the carrot, or the incentive, to learn another language. It may be that hon. members from the province of Quebec would limit themselves to their own language; if we had simultaneous translation, what use would it be to them to learn English? However, I do not think that should bother us here. We have important business to attend to, and I think the initiative of the individual hon. member should be relied upon in these things.
As to the resolution itself, I should say from what we have heard today, that the principle is widely supported in this house, but we would be setting up under this resolution if it were adopted, machinery parallel to that which now exists, and I feel that such an effort would be contrary to the economic use of the services of this house and would respectfully submit that while we agree in principle with the motion, in view of what has been disclosed, either the hon. member who proposed the motion should withdraw it or we should not agree with the motion, and I do so move, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO STUDY SYSTEM OF SIMULTANEOUS TRANSLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is pleasant indeed to enter into a debate in which there is so obvious general agreement on the question of principle. The odd remark I intend to make is really in support of the principle. I had hoped to get across the floor to obtain the notes of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) but as I have some reason to believe that perhaps that hon. gentleman did not understand his own notes he might not be able to help me a great deal.
I think I may say, Mr. Speaker that the agreement which has been expressed here today will be most refreshing to those who read Hansard or other reports of these debates as revealing that an effort is being made in this fine chamber to provide, at some point, members of the House of Commons, not merely with a convenience but with the hope that some day this body will take upon itself a task which many individuals have done to date, namely to learn both languages.
I think that my experience in coming here and recognizing my limitations in speaking

House of Commons
but one language, and making an attempt, as I have done, to speak the other, is one I will reflect upon and look back upon not only with some seriousness but also with some amusement, amusement caused by the fact that my tutor is practically giving me up and has even reached the point of suggesting that the only way I could accomplish my purpose would be by moving across the river, with the implication, of course, that that would not be possible in the circumstances.
I would say, though, that if we are to understand each other in this Canada of ours, and if the two cultures are to grow together, we must have an understanding of each other's language. I think, too, we will agree that once such an understanding has been perfected we can increase in harmony as we have never done before.
It was my experience some years ago when I landed in the Black Lake area of Quebec where there was at that time very little English spoken in the community to find myself in a position which undoubtedly has confronted many others, that of not being able to communicate intelligently with the people who were so kind to me. And, in my particular area of western Canada, I look back on that occasion with some fear and trembling at the prospect that I might not have been able to survive. The fact of the matter is that the people of the Black Lake area were kindness itself.
So, when we come to determine how best to implement this proposal which has been received tonight with general agreement, I do not think the question of what committee shall do the job is actually the most important element before us for consideration. We have received an assurance from a minister of this government that the matter will be given very serious consideration with a view to implementation and I, for one, believe that that is the word of a minister whose intention is honourable and right. I say that, not as a sheep but as a hon. member of this house and I am prepared to support him.
The limitation which some of us suffer, namely, inability to understand each other's language has been used as an example in support of the argument for a simultaneous translation system.
I must confess, however, that there were times when an hon. gentleman across the floor was speaking in French and looking at me, when I felt such a system might well be desirable. The only words I heard him say that I understood were "rock and roll," and then I got a suggestion that "Calgary South" had been used, and I must say I rushed down to mailbox the following morning to see if

it was suggested that I, from Calgary South, had been rocking and rolling. But I found there was no reference to either point.
That is, perhaps, a somewhat facetious way of expressing the limitation. I know, of course, that the people of Canada expect all of us to give this matter consideration so that we can in the future not, as I say, as a convenience but as a matter of necessity, recognize the importance of this type of legislation. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, and as I repeat in conclusion, the important thing is not how we implement this. It is just a question of giving this idea consideration so that it will be put into effect for the benefit of all of us. Once that is done, I feel we can say we are in general agreement, and the motion will, of course, be expedited by all members of this house.

maintopic: ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
subtopic: DISEASE CONTROL OF OYSTER BEDS, KENT COUNTY, N.B.
speechtext:
1.	What steps have been taken towards eliminating the disease prevalent among Kent county, New Brunswick, oyster beds?
2.	What steps have been taken to restock disease-free oysters on Kent county oyster beds?
3.	When is it expected that disease-free oyster fishing in Kent county will be returned to normal?
Answer by: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister
of Fisheries):
1.	Although heavy mortalities were claimed for Cocagne in 1950, Buctouche bay in 1952 and Richibucto in 1950, examinations and field trials did not confirm these until the autumn of 1953 in Buctouche bay. A prohibition was immediately placed on the transfer of oysters or fishing gear from the waters of Kent county to any other.

2.	In 1954 native oysters as well as oysters from Malagash basin, Nova Scotia and Mira-michi bay, New Brunswick, were placed in experimental floating trays. High mortalities appearing in all these oysters in the spring of 1955, was convincing proof of an infectious disease similar to that which decimated the Prince Edward Island stocks in the 1920's.
In 1956, similar tests were made with two to three hundred oysters from Bras d'Or lakes in Nova Scotia. In the spring of 1957 trial plantings were made with about 50 barrels of Prince Edward Island stock considered to be disease resistant. Plans are now almost completed for the transfer of a further one thousand barrels of Prince Edward Island stock to Kent county in 1958.
3.	If the transfer of disease-resistant stock is successful, the oyster fishery in Kent county could return to normal in five to eight years. If the fishery must rebuild from local groups of resistant resident stocks the recovery period could occupy from a minimum of twice the above period to much longer.
Already in Kent county small oysters, apparently from native resistant stocks, are making their appearance. The survivals from trial plantings of Bras d'Or and Prince Edward Island stocks appear very promising especially in Buctouche and Richibucto. If these encouraging results continue and the small oysters are rigidly protected, the recovery period could be much shorter than normal.
